items.prose: `parts` is a list of 50,000 short strings, each 20 characters.
items.question: Which line builds the full report in $O(n)$ time, where $n$ is the total length?

options.why: Each `+=` may copy the whole report so far, which is quadratic in the worst case.
Python refuses `sum` on strings and tells you to use `join`, because repeated `+` is quadratic.

options.text: Build a list with `chars.insert(0, c)`, then join
options.why: Each front insert shifts the whole list, which is quadratic.

feedback.correct: `join` sizes the result once and copies each character once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which version copies each character only once?

explain.text: `"".join(parts)` adds up the lengths, allocates one string and copies each part in once: $O(n)$. Repeated `+=` can recopy the report on every step.

items.prose:
`a` and `b` each hold $n$ tickers.

```python
common = [x for x in a if x in set(b)]
```
items.question: What is the cost of this line?

options.why: The lookup is $O(1)$, but `set(b)` runs inside the comprehension, once per `x`, costing $O(n)$ each time.
Nothing is sorted or halved here. The cost is $n$ set builds of $n$ items each.
The line visits every `x` in `a`, so it is at least $O(n)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How often does `set(b)` run?

explain.text: The condition is evaluated for every `x`, so `set(b)` is built $n$ times. Write `bs = set(b)` first, then `[x for x in a if x in bs]`: $O(n)$.

items.prose: We want a dict key that all anagrams of a word share. Words that are not anagrams must get different keys.
items.question: Which key works?

options.why: A set forgets counts, so `aab` and `ab` would share a key.
Different letters can have equal sums: `ad` and `bc` both give $97 + 100 = 98 + 99$. That is a collision, not a group.
Every word of the same length would share a group, anagram or not.

feedback.correct: Sorted letters keep both which letters and how many.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The key must keep every letter and its count, in a fixed order.

explain.text: Sorting keeps every character, counts included, in one fixed order. So two words share a key exactly when they are anagrams. A sum or a set loses information, so non-anagrams can collide.
